title: Cerebellar Disease: Ocular & Systemic Manifestations
summary: A comprehensive visual guide to the clinical presentation, localization, and diagnostic landscape of cerebellar dysfunction. This poster highlights the critical intersection of ocular motility and motor coordination.

branches: The 'Little Brain': Regulates precision and timing

rows: Downbeat (often Craniocervical junction), Upbeat, Gaze-evoked, or Rebound.
Overshoot (hypermetria) or undershoot (hypometria) when shifting gaze.
Broken, 'cogwheel' or saccadic pursuit instead of smooth tracking.
Spontaneous, back-to-back horizontal saccades without an intersaccadic interval.
Vertical misalignment of the eyes due to asymmetric vestibular input.

content.explanation: D: Dysdiadochokinesia (Impaired rapid alternating movements); A: Ataxia (Gait and limb incoordination); N: Nystagmus (Rhythmic eye oscillation); I: Intention Tremor (Tremor increases near target); S: Slurred Speech (Dysarthria); H: Hypotonia (Reduced muscle tone).

sections.title: Localization of Lesions
content: Vermal Lesions: Result in truncal ataxia, head tilting, and bilateral ocular motor deficits.
Hemispheric Lesions: Result in ipsilateral limb ataxia and dysmetria.
Flocculonodular Lesions: Primarily affect balance and vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression.

sections.title: Urgent Red Flags
content: Sudden Onset Ataxia: Potential cerebellar stroke or hemorrhage.
Papilledema: Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., posterior fossa tumor).
Rapidly Progressive Opsoclonus: May indicate Paraneoplastic Syndrome (e.g., Neuroblastoma in children, Small Cell Lung Cancer in adults).
Acute Vertigo with 'HINTS' positive findings: Differentiating central from peripheral causes.

branches: Toxic: Alcohol, Phenytoin, Chemotherapy, Heavy Metals
Inflammatory/Autoimmune: Multiple Sclerosis, Post-viral Cerebellitis, Gluten Ataxia
Degenerative: Spinocerebellar Ataxias (SCA), Multiple System Atrophy (MSA-C)

sections.title: The Diagnostic Process
content: Step 1: Detailed History (Onset, Duration, Toxic exposure, Family history).
Step 2: Neuro-Ophthalmic Exam (Nystagmus, Saccades, Pursuit, Cover Test).
Step 3: Motor Exam (Finger-to-nose, Heel-to-shin, Rapid alternating movements).
Step 4: Gait Analysis (Tandem gait, Romberg test).
Step 5: Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Posterior Fossa is the Gold Standard).
Step 6: Laboratory Testing (Genetic panels, Paraneoplastic markers, Vitamin levels).

sections.title: Verbatim Clinical Context
sections.content: Cerebellar disease represents a broad spectrum of disorders where the primary deficit is the loss of motor control and coordination. While the cerebellum does not initiate movement, it acts as a critical 'comparator'—adjusting motor output by comparing intended movement with actual sensory feedback. In ophthalmology, this manifest as 'dysmetria of thought' and eye movement, where the brain cannot accurately calibrate the magnitude of saccades or the smoothness of tracking, leading to visual instability and vertigo.
